title: What must companies in Japan do to prevent harassment of freelancers under the Freelance Act?
description: Japan's Freelance Act Article 14: harassment measures for freelancers since November 1, 2024, the MHLW Guideline, staff training and evidence.
shortAnswer: Since November 1, 2024, Article 14 of Japan's Act on Ensuring Proper Transactions Involving Specified Entrusted Business Operators requires any business with employees that commissions work from a solo freelancer to take measures against sexual, maternity and power harassment of that freelancer. The Ministry of Health, Labour and Welfare Guideline requires a communicated policy, a consultation desk, prompt response and privacy protection, and names training as a way to inform staff.
keyTakeaways: The duty sits in Article 14 of Act No. 25 of 2023 (Tokutei Jutaku Jigyōsha ni Kakaru Torihiki no Tekiseika Tō ni Kansuru Hōritsu), in force November 1, 2024.
It applies to a commissioning business that has employees, or a company with two or more officers, whenever it engages a freelancer who has no employees, regardless of contract length.

The MHLW Guideline (MHLW Notice No. 212 of 2024, last amended February 26, 2026) requires the harassment policy to reach contract managers, project staff, people who inspect deliverables and people who work alongside freelancers.
Training is listed as an accepted way to communicate the policy, to prepare consultation desk staff and to prevent recurrence.
Breaches can lead to a recommendation and, if ignored, publication of the company's name. Failing to answer a report request carries a non-penal fine of up to 200,000 yen.
regulator: Ministry of Health, Labour and Welfare (MHLW) and Prefectural Labor Bureaus for Chapter 3 working environment duties; Japan Fair Trade Commission (JFTC) and the Small and Medium Enterprise Agency for transaction terms
appliesTo: Businesses with at least one employee (or companies with two or more officers) that commission goods, digital content or services from a freelancer with no employees
Contract managers, project leads and procurement staff who deal with freelancers
Staff who check, inspect or accept freelancers' deliverables
Employees who work side by side with freelancers
Consultation desk and HR staff who receive harassment reports

sections.heading: Which law creates the freelancer harassment duty in Japan?

blocks.text: The duty comes from **Article 14** of the Act on Ensuring Proper Transactions Involving Specified Entrusted Business Operators (Act No. 25 of 2023), usually called the Freelance Act. The law took effect on November 1, 2024, a date the MHLW confirms on its [Freelance Act information page](https://www.mhlw.go.jp/stf/seisakunitsuite/bunya/koyou_roudou/koyoukintou/zaitaku/index_00002.html). As at November 2026, Chapter 3 of the Act covers the freelancer's working environment and is enforced by the MHLW through Prefectural Labor Bureaus.

Article 14(1) requires the commissioning business to set up a system to respond to consultations and to take other necessary measures so that a freelancer's working environment is not harmed by three kinds of conduct. Article 15 directs the Minister of Health, Labour and Welfare to publish a guideline, and the current text is MHLW Notice No. 212 of May 31, 2024, amended by Notice No. 53 of February 26, 2026, published as the [MHLW Guideline](https://www.mhlw.go.jp/content/001318005.pdf). The [statutory text on e-Gov](https://laws.e-gov.go.jp/law/505AC0000000025) is the authority for every article cited here.

Employers already run measures for their own staff under the Equal Employment Opportunity Act and the [power harassment prevention duty](/regulations/japan-power-harassment-prevention-obligations). The Freelance Act extends a parallel set of measures to people who are not employees at all, which is why many companies need to revisit who their policy actually covers.

sections.heading: Which businesses and freelancers does Article 14 cover?

blocks.text: Article 14 covers any commissioning business that uses employees or, for a company, has two or more officers, whenever it engages a freelancer. The Act calls the freelancer a specified entrusted business operator (tokutei jutaku jigyōsha) and defines it in Article 2(1) as an individual who uses no employees, or a company whose only officer is its representative and which uses no employees.

The commissioning side is a specified commissioning business operator (tokutei gyōmu itaku jigyōsha) under Article 2(6). Unlike the mandatory part of Article 13 and the notice duty in Article 16, which apply only to engagements that continue beyond a period set by Cabinet Order, Article 14 has no minimum contract length. A one-day photography job or a short translation is enough to bring the duty into play.

blocks.caption: How the Article 2 definitions decide whether Article 14 applies

blocks.text: Article 14(1) targets sexual harassment, harassment related to pregnancy or childbirth, and power harassment based on a superior transactional relationship. Each is framed around the freelancer's position as a contractor rather than an employee.

items: **Sexual harassment (item 1):** sexual conduct that leads to worse contract terms when the freelancer objects, or that harms the freelancer's working environment.
**Pregnancy and childbirth harassment (item 2):** conduct about pregnancy or childbirth matters specified by MHLW ordinance that harms the working environment.
**Power harassment (item 3):** conduct backed by a superior position in the transaction that goes beyond what is necessary and appropriate for the work and harms the working environment.

blocks.text: The Guideline gives contract specific examples of power harassment. They include forcing physically or mentally demanding work not contemplated by the contract, making the freelancer run private errands unrelated to the engagement, and repeatedly rejecting deliverables to harass the freelancer without stating clear acceptance criteria. It also lists conduct that is not harassment, such as asking for rework of the parts that fall short of acceptance criteria that were clearly stated in advance.

Article 14(2) adds a retaliation ban: the business must not terminate the contract or otherwise treat the freelancer unfavorably because they consulted about harassment or gave facts during an investigation.

sections.heading: What measures does the MHLW Guideline require?

blocks.text: Section 4, part 5 of the Guideline requires four groups of measures: a clear policy that staff are told about, a consultation system, a prompt response to each case, and supporting protections for privacy and against retaliation. These are mandatory for every covered business; the Guideline uses the phrase "must take" (kōjinakereba naranai).

items: **Policy and awareness.** Define what harassment in commissioned work means, state that it must not happen, and set disciplinary rules for anyone who does it. The policy must reach staff including contract and project managers, people who check or accept deliverables, and people who work alongside freelancers.

**Consultation system.** Set up a consultation desk in advance and tell freelancers about it, for example by printing the contact in the contract document or email. An existing employee harassment desk may be extended to freelancers. Desk staff must be able to respond appropriately, including to borderline cases.

**Response after a report.** Establish the facts quickly and accurately, take measures for the freelancer, take measures toward the person responsible, and take steps to prevent recurrence even when the facts cannot be confirmed.

**Privacy and no retaliation.** Protect the privacy of everyone involved, including sensitive information such as sexual orientation, gender identity, medical history and fertility treatment, and tell freelancers that they will not lose the contract for consulting or for reporting to the MHLW.

blocks.text: Section 6 of the Guideline adds a desirable step: extend the same policy to people who are still negotiating a contract. Section 7 recommends measures against harassment of freelancers by other businesses and by customers, and says that preparing manuals and running training on how to respond is also effective.

sections.heading: Is training mandatory under the Freelance Act?

blocks.text: Training is not mandatory in its own right, but it is one of the Guideline's named ways of meeting mandatory measures, and in practice it is hard to show that the policy reached the right staff without it. The Guideline mentions training (kenshū) or lectures (kōshū) in three places within the required measures.

items: As an example of communicating the policy: running training or lectures to inform workers of what harassment in commissioned work is and that it must not occur.
As an example of enabling the consultation desk: training desk staff on how to respond when they receive a consultation, and training them on privacy protection.
As an example of recurrence prevention: running awareness training or lectures for employees again after a case.

blocks.text: The MHLW has also produced free training videos through its freelance working environment project, published on its [training video page](https://www.mhlw.go.jp/stf/seisakunitsuite/bunya/koyou_roudou/koyoukintou/zaitaku/freelance_00007.html): one for commissioning businesses (31 minutes 20 seconds), one for harassment consultation desk staff (49 minutes 7 seconds), and one for the advertising industry (38 minutes 33 seconds). The ministry invites companies to use them for in-house training.

Because the Guideline names specific audiences, a generic employee harassment module is unlikely to be enough on its own. It needs content on the freelancer relationship: acceptance criteria, rework requests, scope creep, payment pressure and how a freelancer can raise a concern.

sections.heading: What happens if a company does not comply?

blocks.text: The MHLW can recommend corrective action under Article 18 and, if the company ignores a recommendation about Article 14 without good reason, publish that fact under Article 19(3). Unlike other Freelance Act duties, Article 14 breaches cannot lead to an order or to a criminal fine for ignoring one.

For Article 14 matters the Minister can require reports under Article 20(2). Under Article 26, a company that fails to report or reports falsely faces a non-penal administrative fine (karyō) of up to 200,000 yen. A freelancer can also notify the Minister of a breach under Article 17, and the Minister must investigate. Article 23 allows these powers to be delegated to Prefectural Labor Bureau directors.

Freelancers are using these channels. In the [MHLW enforcement summary for fiscal 2025](https://www.mhlw.go.jp/content/001731548.pdf), Labor Bureaus received 1,895 consultations under the Act, of which 471 (17.5%) concerned the harassment system duty in Article 14. In the first partial year, from November 1, 2024 to March 31, 2025, there were 1,301 consultations, 304 of them (16.8%) about Article 14.

sections.heading: How should a company build Freelance Act harassment training?

blocks.text: Start from the roles the Guideline names, not from the whole workforce. Most organizations already train employees on workplace harassment, so the gap is usually the small group of people who commission, manage and accept freelance work.

items: Identify every team that engages freelancers, including marketing, IT, design, events and content, and list the roles that brief, manage or accept their work.
Extend the harassment policy and disciplinary rules to cover freelancers explicitly, and record the change date.
Add the consultation desk contact and the no retaliation statement to engagement templates.
Build a short module for freelancer facing roles with scenarios drawn from the Guideline's examples, such as rework without clear criteria and private errands.
Train consultation desk staff on accepting reports from non-employees, privacy, and coordinating with the contract owner.
Schedule a refresher after any substantiated case, since the Guideline treats renewed awareness training as a recurrence prevention measure.

blocks.text: For the mechanics of assigning modules to roles, see [how to build a training matrix](/guides/how-to-build-a-training-matrix) and [how to map training to compliance obligations](/guides/how-to-map-training-to-compliance-obligations). Companies whose staff also face customers should align this module with the [customer harassment duties that took effect in October 2026](/regulations/japan-customer-harassment-prevention-obligations).

sections.heading: How does Knowledge Foundry approach this?

blocks.text: Knowledge Foundry records Article 14 and each Guideline measure as separate obligations linked to the roles the Guideline names, so a contract manager's learning outcomes differ from a consultation desk handler's. Each outcome carries an assessment point and a source reference to the dated Guideline version, which makes the February 2026 amendment traceable in the training record.

faqs.q: Does the Freelance Act apply to foreign companies engaging freelancers in Japan?
faqs.a: The Act regulates commissioning businesses that meet the Article 2(6) definition, and the MHLW enforces it in Japan. A company engaging freelancers for work in Japan should assume Article 14 applies and seek local advice on its specific structure. The duties attach to the engagement, not to the freelancer's nationality.

faqs.q: Can we use our existing employee harassment hotline for freelancers?
faqs.a: Yes. The Guideline expressly allows an existing consultation desk set up for employee sexual, maternity or power harassment to be made available for harassment in commissioned work. The desk must then be notified to freelancers, for example in the contract email, and desk staff must be able to handle reports from non-employees.

faqs.q: Does the duty apply if the freelancer works through a platform or agency?
faqs.a: Article 14 applies to the business that commissions the freelancer directly. Where the freelancer works at another company's premises, Section 7 of the Guideline recommends agreeing in the contract that the host will also take harassment measures and cooperate with fact finding. That is a recommended step, not a mandatory one.

faqs.q: Is there a size threshold for the Freelance Act harassment duty?
faqs.a: No headcount threshold applies. A commissioning business with a single employee, or a company with two officers, meets the definition in Article 2(6). Individuals and one person companies with no employees are outside the Chapter 3 duties when they commission work themselves.
